title: Implement a trie, also called a prefix tree, supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix. Explain the Trie pattern, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree with Insert, Search, and StartsWith)

s1_definition.profdef: A trie is the core data structure of the Trie pattern, a tree where each edge represents one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Each node holds child links and a flag marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all walk the tree one character at a time, so each runs in time proportional to the key length, independent of how many keys are stored.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A trie is the core data structure of the Trie pattern, a tree where each edge represents one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Each node holds child links and a flag marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all walk the tree one character at a time, so each runs in time proportional to the key length, independent of how many keys are stored.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India stores a large set of registered merchant names and wants to look up names and check prefixes quickly as a teller types. A trie stores shared prefixes once, so RELIANCE and RELIABLE share the same early branch, making lookups fast and memory efficient.

**One line to remember:** A trie stores characters along edges so every key operation costs only the length of the key.

sections.s2_technical:
Each trie node has an array or map of child links, one slot per possible character, and a boolean marking the end of a complete word. To insert a word we start at the root and for each character follow the matching child, creating it if it does not exist, and after the last character we set the end flag. To search for a complete word we walk the same path and succeed only if every character has a link and the final node has its end flag set. To check a prefix we walk the path and succeed as long as every character has a link, regardless of the end flag.

The insert core is `TrieNode node = root; for (char c : word.toCharArray()) { node = node.children.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new TrieNode()); } node.isWord = true;`. Search and prefix share a traversal helper that returns the node reached, then search checks the end flag while prefix just checks the node exists. A concrete check: after inserting RELIANCE, searching RELIANCE succeeds, searching RELI fails as a word but succeeds as a prefix. Senior nuance: operations are order of the key length, memory can be reduced with a compressed radix tree, and a character map scales better than a fixed array for large alphabets.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores a large set of registered merchant names and a teller needs to look up whether a typed name is registered and whether any registered name starts with what has been typed so far, with instant response. Scanning a flat list on every keystroke is slow. This is exactly how a trie works: it stores shared prefixes once and answers each lookup in time proportional only to the typed length.

The code defines a `MerchantTrie` with `insert(name)`, `search(name)`, and `startsWith(prefix)`, plus a supporting `TrieNode`. A `Demo` inserts a few merchant names and logs the results of searches and prefix checks.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is inserting RELIANCE and RELIABLE, then searching RELIANCE, searching RELI, and checking the prefix RELI.

Step 1 — Inserting RELIANCE walks from the root creating nodes for R, E, L, I, A, N, C, E, and marks the final E node as the end of a word.

Step 2 — Inserting RELIABLE reuses the shared branch R, E, L, I, then creates A, B, L, E, marking the final E as the end of a word. The shared prefix RELI is stored only once.

Step 3 — Searching RELIANCE walks the full path and finds the end flag set on the last node, so it returns true.

Step 4 — Searching RELI walks to the I node, which exists but has no end flag because no complete name ends there, so it returns false.

Step 5 — Checking the prefix RELI walks to the same I node, which exists, so the prefix check returns true. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:57:08 PM com.bank.merchtrie.MerchantTrieApplication main
INFO: search RELIANCE = true
Oct 27, 2026 9:57:08 PM com.bank.merchtrie.MerchantTrieApplication main
INFO: search RELI = false
Oct 27, 2026 9:57:08 PM com.bank.merchtrie.MerchantTrieApplication main
INFO: startsWith RELI = true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Insert "RELIANCE", "RELIABLE"
    │
    ▼
  root → R → E → L → I ─┬─ A → N → C → E(isWord)
                        └─ A → B → L → E(isWord)
    │ shared prefix RELI stored once
    ▼
  search("RELIANCE") → path ends at isWord → true
  search("RELI")     → node exists but isWord=false → false
  startsWith("RELI") → node exists → true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A trie, or prefix tree, is the core data structure of the Trie pattern, and I describe it as a tree where each edge carries one character so that the path from the root to any node spells a prefix. Every node keeps links to its children and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends at that node. The beauty is that shared prefixes are stored exactly once, so two names that begin the same way share their early branch.

To insert a word I walk from the root following or creating a child for each character and set the end flag on the final node. To search for a complete word I walk the same path and succeed only if every character has a link and the final node has its end flag set. To check a prefix I walk the path and succeed as long as every character has a link, ignoring the end flag. Because each operation follows one link per character, they all cost time proportional to the key length, independent of how many keys are stored, which is the trie's defining advantage.

At the National Bank of India I used a trie to store registered merchant names so a teller could instantly check whether a typed name was registered and whether any registered name started with the typed prefix. I warmed the trie from the database at startup and served every keystroke from memory. Explaining that characters live on edges, that the end-of-word flag separates a complete name from a mere prefix, and that each operation costs only the key length is what shows an interviewer I understand the Trie pattern.
